rationale: Evidence: iteration 3 is still the best design (score 697.4). Its oval (20/20, 1.84 s) and s-bend (20/20, 2.08 s) both finish cleanly. The slalom is the only failure: 20/20 off-track exits at mean progress 0.48, with one line-loss event per run and max_error at the 0.06 m limit. Iteration 4 tried to fix the slalom by raising kp 3.5 to 4.0, kd 1.6 to 2.0 and widening the sensor spread to +/-0.06. That made things worse: slalom progress fell to 0.17, s-bend finishes fell to 16/20, and steering oscillation rose. So the extra steering gain and the wider spread are not the fix. The most likely limit is speed on the sharp slalom reversals: at base_speed 1.2 the robot carries too much momentum to turn the reversal and loses the tape. Change: revert to the iteration 3 controller and geometry (kp 3.5, kd 1.6, ki 0.02, sensor spread +/-0.05 at y 0.07, sensor_size 0.016, mass 0.6) and lower base_speed from 1.2 to 1.0. This is the only change, so its effect can be read directly. Time budget: the oval took 1.84 s at 1.2, so at 1.0 it should take roughly 2.2 s, and the s-bend roughly 2.5 s, both under the 3 s limit. The time term is small, so the score cost is limited. Expected result: slalom progress rises above 0.6 and some slalom runs finish, while the oval and s-bend keep 20/20 finishes. Hypotheses: (a) slalom exits are caused by overshoot at reversals at speed, not by steering authority; (b) if slalom progress does not improve at base_speed 1.0, the limit is sensor coverage at the reversal, and the next step is a sensor_size or spread change alone. Measurements to check next: per-track completion and progress, slalom line_loss_events, max_error location, completion_time on the oval and s-bend (to confirm the time budget), and steering_oscillation.
